verification: UNVERIFIED: written from memory of Diamond, McQuade and Qian (2019), AER 109(9); the paper could not be fetched from this environment. Every figure must be checked against the paper, and the card checked by a second person, before this case counts.

findings.magnitude: treated tenants roughly 10-20% more likely to remain at their 1994 address
rental housing supply of treated buildings down about 15%
more conversion to condominiums and tenancies-in-common, sale to owner-occupiers, redevelopment

findings.note: model-based estimate from the supply reduction, not a direct comparison

assumption_status.evidence: Market rents rose far faster than 60% of CPI in the late 1990s (to be sourced).
Treated tenants stayed longer, which requires the limit to be applied (F-1).
Treated tenants were less likely to leave San Francisco (F-2), which needs some to have left otherwise.

confounders: Dot-com boom of the late 1990s and later technology booms raised demand for housing citywide
Ellis Act withdrawals and changes to condominium conversion rules over the period
